question: Each trial has a probability of success of \(1/2\), and the 2 trials do not affect each other. What is the probability that both trials succeed?
solution: Given that the first trial succeeds, the probability of success on the second trial is still \(1/2\). Multiplying gives \(1/4\).

nodes.description: Construct and interpret two-way frequency tables of data when two categories are associated with each object being classified. Use the two-way table as a sample space to decide if events are independent and to approximate conditional probabilities. For example, collect data from a random sample of students in your school on their favorite subject among math, science, and English. edges.reason: The explicit independence/exclusivity contrast requires mutual exclusivity.
Repeated independent probabilities use the product relation.
The defining formula P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B) uses the intersection event, and stating the definition is a mastery criterion. The P(B)>0 condition is a node content fix, not edge scope.
edges.scope: meaning of A∩B in the definition

edges.reason: The independent-event product is a familiar special case. The general rule follows directly by rearranging conditional probability, with positive conditioning probability, rather than requiring the earlier independent-repeat workflow.
edges.scope: product rule as generalization of independent case

edges.reason: The multiplication identity uses the conditional probability P(B given A). Its meaning and the positive probability of the conditioning event are necessary to this conditional form.

The product definition supplies useful comparison with the conditional characterization. Independence and its difference from mutual exclusivity can also be introduced directly through unchanged conditional probability, so the older product-definition lesson is preparation.
edges.scope: linking conditional criterion to product definition

edges.reason: The criterion tests independence by comparing P(B given A) and P(B). Understanding conditional probability is necessary for this specified test when P(A) is positive.

The integer-multiplier case supplies a useful stepping stone and repeated-addition interpretation. The product-of-numerators/product-of-denominators rule follows directly from a part-of-a-part area model without executing the earlier decimal-free integer-multiplier procedure; Gemini confuses this customary progression with necessity.
